> Red-team review of f6de5c1fe (K5 6/8), in a scratch worktree (removed). As package reviewer I also decide the numeric target, and I ran a local diagnostic for the R5 question.

> (1) CODE: OK with notes.
> - Trace absent from default builds: verified on both widths. I built redoubt-kernel --release --features qemu-virt for riscv64imac and riscv32imac: 'SCHED-TRACE' strings 0, sched::trace symbols 0, tie_fault symbols 0. With sched-trace on rv64: 2 strings and 3 symbols. Only sched-ties and sched-latency enable it.
> - The oracle is independent. It rebuilds rank keys from events alone: (0, -entry) for a wake, (1, n) for the n-th requeue, then the id; no tie key crosses. It rejects a pick that is not the rank minimum, as well as malformed, incomplete, dropped and pick-less traces.
> - The negative run's evidence comes from the fault feature: the oracle names the record, and the in-guest clause-2/3 checks fail with the same feature.
> - Ring: 10240 x 16 B; any drop fails the case.
> Notes:
> (a) The oracle trusts the recorded pass values, so it checks only the order of picks given the passes. Floor, charging and lift arithmetic are unchecked at boot (this is why review-3 T2 is still owed). A cheap independent addition: track a monotone floor in the oracle (min over queued passes) and require every W record's pass >= that floor and every budget's pass never to fall. That would have caught the no-floor plant from review 3 independently.
> (b) id_kind stores id << 8 in a u32, so budget ids above 2^24 alias. Assert it, or widen the record.
> (c) Clauses 1 and 4 are never exercised on target (only 2 and 3). The host tests, model traces and fault run cover them; state that in the case.
> (d) With the larger K I require below, re-size the ring or it will drop: about 5x the picks, plus W/R/D/P records.
> 
> (2) TARGET DECISION: AMEND, then accept on re-measurement.
> - Sample size. K = 40 wakes gives 'p99 = max', and 8 destroys of each kind support no percentile at all. Before pinning, re-measure with K >= 200 wakes per N (report p99 as the 2nd largest of 200) and >= 50 destroys of each kind, on rv64 and rv32. Virtual time makes this cheap.
> - Also owed from plan s12/K5-q-bench and not in this commit: the plain-TCG reference run (5 repetitions, with spread).
> - Pin only if the re-measurement meets the targets below. Otherwise come back with numbers.
> Targets (virtual instruction time, icount shift=3, QEMU virt, this named workload with stand-ins at INIT.md weights, N <= 16):
>   T-a. Driver wake and steward timer wake: p99 <= 50 ms, as proposed, and also p50 <= 15 ms. A p99-only target misses a common-case regression: for example, every wake waiting two slices would still pass 50 ms. Measured p50 is 9-11 ms, max 32.5/43.2.
>   T-b. Deadline notice: p99 <= 30 ms, as proposed. It is R10's cost plus under 1 ms, and R10 grows with the frames present, so record the object and frame counts with the table. Tie this to follow-up K5-r10-destroy-cost: once R10 is indexed, tighten to about 10 ms.
>   T-c. NEW, steward-initiated termination (TENETS guarantee 3). The lease is dead when R10 finishes inside the budget_destroy call. The 222 ms maximum is the steward's CPU wait after that, when its slice ended during R10: it delays the steward's next action, not the lease's death.
>     (i) budget_destroy kernel time, call entry to R10 complete: p99 <= 30 ms, the same bound as the deadline path. Measure it separately from the CPU wait, e.g. an R10 start/end record in the sched-trace ring, or the N=1 call-to-return.
>     (ii) Lease termination from the steward's decision (its timer deadline) to the lease's processes killed, = steward wake + (i): p99 <= 80 ms.
>     (iii) budget_destroy call-to-return, including the CPU wait: record it, don't assert it, and state its bound as one round: <= 30 ms + (runnable + 2) x SLICE (about 220 ms at N=16), the same discrete-round residual as K5-debt-lift-bound. rv32's 62 ms against rv64's 222 ms at N=16 shows it depends on phase.
>   T-d. Server share >= its weight share - 30/1000: accepted (381 and 373 against 384).
> - Margin: R10's non-preemptible 13-20 ms dominates T-b and T-c(i), and it sits under every wake's tail. The margins (30 against about 21; 50 against 43) are adequate for this workload only. Note in the target text that adding objects moves them, and gate any growth on the K5-r10-destroy-cost follow-up.
> 
> (3) R5 'lost interrupt' observation: partly reproduced, not 'never', and not proven to be a kernel bug. Assign it to K3, not K5.
> My local diagnostic (the driver stand-in, rv64, reverted afterwards). Six trials, each: arm the RTC alarm 1 ms ahead, spin 3 ms (so it rises while the IRQ object is masked), then receive with a 50 ms timeout; then clear, arm an alarm already past, and receive again.
> - The masked-raise receive was lost only on trial 0 (the driver's first receive after the launcher's find() probing and the handle handover). Trials 1-5 were delivered.
> - The fresh-edge receive was delivered 6/6.
> So 'an alarm raised while masked is never delivered' is overstated: there is a first-time or state-dependent loss.
> Reading the kernel path (device::irq_fired, message::receive_irq, intc_plic): the initial IRQ object is masked=true and the first receive enables it. irq_fired completes the PLIC claim (enable_all_irqs), then disables the source. That order is required, because the PLIC ignores completes for a disabled source, and it means a still-asserted level source re-pends at complete. I found no kernel defect by reading. Candidates: QEMU sifive_plic's pending semantics for a level line that falls while disabled, or stale state left by find() probing other IRQ handles (those receives time out and leave their sources unmasked).
> Owner: K3 (IRQ objects, R5), as a follow-up with a dedicated boot case (irq-level-latch): for a level source, raise while masked, then receive. It must deliver on every trial, including the first after a handle handover, and read the PLIC pending bit to tell the kernel apart from QEMU.
> D3 impact: netd's rx IRQ can fire between receives. Until the K3 case passes, netd must do what virtio drivers do anyway: after each receive (re-enable), re-check the used ring before sleeping again, so a lost or coalesced interrupt costs latency, not packets. Tell D3.
>
